title: Sindhi Biryani
tagline: Spicier and tangier than most — with potatoes, prunes and a bright hit of chilli.
intro: Sindhi biryani is the fiery, tangy pride of Sindh. What sets it apart is the balance of heat and sourness — plenty of green chilli and dried plum (aloo bukhara), potatoes tucked between the layers, and a generous scatter of mint. It is arguably Pakistan's most iconic street and home biryani.

items: 1 cinnamon stick, 4 cloves, 4 green cardamom, 1 bay leaf
1 kg chicken or mutton, cut into pieces
Large handful of mint and coriander, chopped
½ tsp saffron or yellow colour in 3 tbsp milk

method: Rinse and soak the basmati for 30 minutes; drain.
Fry the onions in oil until golden. Add ginger–garlic paste and green chillies, then the meat, and sear.
Add the ground spices, biryani masala, tomatoes and salt. Cook until the oil separates.
Stir in yoghurt, add the potatoes, cover and cook until the meat and potatoes are tender. Add the dried plums in the last 5 minutes. The masala should be thick and tangy.
Boil the rice water with salt and whole spices; parboil the rice to 70% and drain.
Layer rice over the masala, scattering mint, coriander, fried onions, saffron milk and kewra water between two layers.
Seal and steam (dum) on the lowest heat for 20–25 minutes.
Rest 5 minutes and fold gently before serving.
tips: The dried plums are essential — they give Sindhi biryani its signature tang.
Keep the chilli generous; this biryani is meant to be lively and hot.
toServe: Best with cooling raita and sliced onions.
